title: Chapter 114 — Crossing Over: From Top Seller to Sales Leader
intro: The job changes completely. What made you the best salesperson will not make you the best manager.

sections.title: The First Mistake Every New Manager Makes
sections.content:
The first mistake is trying to be the best salesperson on the team. That was your old job. Your new job is making everyone else better.

The skills that got you promoted — closing, presenting, building relationships — are still valuable. But now they are tools you use to teach, not to sell. If you keep jumping in to close your team's deals, you are not managing. You are doing their job while neglecting yours.

sections.title: The Ex-Peer Problem
sections.content:
Yesterday you were peers. Today you are the boss. That is awkward for everyone.

Do not pretend the dynamic has not changed. Acknowledge it directly. Set expectations early. Be fair, consistent, and professional. Some friendships will adjust. Some will not. That is the cost of leadership.

The worst thing you can do is play favorites with your old friends. The team sees everything. Inconsistency destroys credibility faster than any single mistake.

sections.title: Your New Metrics
sections.content:
As a salesperson, your metric was personal production. As a manager, your metric is team production.

You succeed when the team succeeds. You fail when the team fails — even if you could have personally outsold everyone. That is the hardest mental shift in the transition.

Great managers build stronger teams. Weak managers rely on stronger individuals.

sections.title: Coaching Rule
sections.content:
When evaluating new managers, ask:

Are they coaching the team — or still trying to be the top seller?
Have they addressed the peer-to-boss transition directly?
Do they measure success by team performance — not personal production?
Are they fair and consistent — or playing favorites?
